excerpt: AP is one of the most predictable scorers in the Class 10 board paper — if you get two formulas right and stop making three silly mistakes. Here is the full chapter, the board problem types, and a quiz to check yourself.
author: Sachin Sharma
content:
Look at 3, 7, 11, 15, 19. Each number is 4 more than the one before it. That constant step is the whole idea behind an Arithmetic Progression, and the Class 10 chapter on it is, in my experience marking board-style papers, one of the easiest 6–8 marks a student can bank — provided they nail two formulas and stop repeating the same three careless errors. This guide walks through the full CBSE chapter: what an AP actually is, the nth term, both sum formulas, the word problems that show up every year, and the mistakes that quietly cost marks.

What is an Arithmetic Progression?

An Arithmetic Progression is a list of numbers where the difference between any term and the one before it is always the same. That fixed gap is called the common difference, written d. The first term is a.

For 3, 7, 11, 15: the first term a = 3 and d = 7 − 3 = 4. To check whether a sequence is an AP, subtract each term from the next; if you get the same number every time, it is an AP. Note that d can be negative (the AP decreases, like 20, 17, 14…) or zero (a constant list like 5, 5, 5…).

  • Increasing AP: d is positive — 2, 5, 8, 11 (d = 3)
  • Decreasing AP: d is negative — 10, 7, 4, 1 (d = −3)
  • Constant AP: d = 0 — 6, 6, 6, 6

The nth term: a + (n − 1)d

You do not want to list out 50 terms to find the 50th. The nth term formula gives it directly:

an = a + (n − 1)d

Here a is the first term, d the common difference, and n the position you want. For the AP 3, 7, 11, 15… the 20th term is a20 = 3 + (20 − 1) × 4 = 3 + 76 = 79.

The most common board question type

Boards love to flip this around: they give you a term and ask for n, or give two terms and ask for a and d. Example: if the 7th term is 34 and the 13th term is 64, find the AP. Write both as equations — a + 6d = 34 and a + 12d = 64 — subtract to get 6d = 30, so d = 5 and a = 4. The AP is 4, 9, 14, 19… This two-equation trick solves a huge share of AP questions.

Sum of n terms: two formulas, one chapter

The sum of the first n terms of an AP, written Sn, has two forms. Use whichever fits the information you are given.

Sn = n/2 [2a + (n − 1)d] — use when you know a, d and n.

Sn = n/2 (a + l) — use when you know the first term a and the last term l. Here l is just an, the last term.

Say you want the sum of the first 20 terms of 3, 7, 11… With a = 3, d = 4, n = 20: S20 = 20/2 [2×3 + 19×4] = 10 [6 + 76] = 10 × 82 = 820. The second formula is a gift when the last term is handed to you — for "sum of all two-digit numbers divisible by 3" you know the first (12) and last (99) terms, so S = n/2 (a + l) is far quicker.

You are givenUse this formulaWhy
a, d, nSn = n/2 [2a + (n−1)d]No need to find the last term first

Word problems: where AP earns its marks

The application questions look intimidating but almost all reduce to spotting a and d. Three patterns turn up again and again in CBSE papers.

Savings and instalments

"Rekha saves ₹100 in the first month and increases her saving by ₹50 each month. How much does she save in the 12th month, and in total over a year?" Here a = 100, d = 50. The 12th month is a12 = 100 + 11×50 = ₹650, and the yearly total is S12 = 12/2 [200 + 11×50] = 6 × 750 = ₹4,500.

Seats in an auditorium

"A hall has 20 seats in the first row, 24 in the second, 28 in the third, and so on for 15 rows." That is an AP with a = 20, d = 4. Total seats = S15 = 15/2 [40 + 14×4] = 7.5 × 96 = 720.

Salary increments

"A man starts on an annual salary of ₹3,00,000 with a fixed raise of ₹15,000 every year. What is his salary in the 10th year?" a = 300000, d = 15000, so a10 = 300000 + 9×15000 = ₹4,35,000. Read the wording carefully: "in the 10th year" means the 10th term, not the ninth.

Common mistakes that cost marks

  • Using n instead of (n − 1). The nth term is a + (n−1)d, not a + nd. This single slip is the biggest mark-loser in the chapter.
  • Getting the sign of d wrong in a decreasing AP. For 25, 20, 15… d is −5, not 5.
  • Confusing "nth term" with "sum of n terms". Read whether the question wants one value (an) or a running total (Sn).
  • Off-by-one in counting terms — for numbers from 12 to 99 in steps of 3, n = (99 − 12)/3 + 1 = 30, and forgetting the "+ 1" is a classic error.

Test yourself, then get exam-style practice

Below is a free 8-question quiz covering exactly these ideas — nth term, both sum formulas and a couple of word problems. Try each one, then read the worked explanation for anything you miss. When you are ready for full board-style practice, the case-study workbook linked at the end gives you AP problems in the paragraph-based format CBSE now uses, each with a complete solution.

quiz.title: Class 10 Arithmetic Progression Quiz
quiz.intro: Eight questions on the nth term, sum formulas and AP word problems, pitched at CBSE Class 10 level. Choose an answer for each, then press Check my score.

questions.q: What is the common difference of the AP 7, 11, 15, 19, ...?
questions.explanation: Subtract any term from the next: 11 − 7 = 4. The common difference d = 4.

questions.q: For the AP with first term 5 and common difference 3, what is the 10th term?
Which formula gives the sum of n terms when you know the first term a and the last term l?
questions.explanation: When the first and last terms are known, S_n = n/2 (a + l) is the quickest form.

questions.q: Find the sum of the first 15 terms of the AP 2, 5, 8, 11, ...
The 5th term of an AP is 19 and the 9th term is 35. What is the common difference?
questions.explanation: a + 8d = 35 and a + 4d = 19. Subtracting: 4d = 16, so d = 4.

questions.q: How many two-digit numbers are divisible by 3?
A hall has 18 seats in row 1, 22 in row 2, 26 in row 3, and so on. How many seats are in row 10?
Anita saves ₹200 in month 1 and ₹50 more each month. How much does she save in total over 6 months?

faq.q: What is the difference between the nth term and the sum of n terms in an AP?
faq.a: The nth term (a<sub>n</sub>) is the single value at position n, found with a + (n−1)d. The sum of n terms (S<sub>n</sub>) is the running total of all terms up to position n, found with n/2 [2a + (n−1)d]. Read each question to see which one it asks for.

faq.q: Which sum formula should I use in the Class 10 exam?
faq.a: Use S<sub>n</sub> = n/2 [2a + (n−1)d] when you know the first term, common difference and number of terms. Switch to S<sub>n</sub> = n/2 (a + l) when the last term is given — it needs less arithmetic and leaves fewer chances to slip.

faq.q: Can the common difference be negative or zero?
faq.a: Yes. A negative d gives a decreasing AP such as 20, 17, 14, and a d of zero gives a constant list such as 5, 5, 5. Both are still valid arithmetic progressions, and boards do test the negative-d case.

faq.q: How much of the Class 10 board paper does AP usually cover?
faq.a: Arithmetic Progression is a dedicated chapter and typically carries around 6 to 8 marks across short-answer, long-answer and case-study questions. Because the question types repeat every year, it is one of the most reliable chapters to score full marks in.
